item.title: Revisiting the Fermi Paradox: Does the Math Hold up?
item.description: arXiv:2611.28075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a stochastic model to address the famous Fermi Paradox, i.e. the supposed contradiction between the abundance of intelligent life in the universe and the absence of any evidence of it. The model assumes that life can arise and evolve on habitable planets with a certain chance, and that we can detect life on other planets within a certain distance. The parameters of the model include the rates, at which life arises, evolves, vanishes, or advances to "Space Age", i.e. a stage where it gains the capability of interstellar communication. Given any numerical choice of these parameters, the model estimates a Contact Probability, i.e. the probability of having received a signal from an extraterrestrial civilization during the ongoing Space Age on Earth. Based on a critical probability threshold, the model can identify regions in the parameter space where Contact Probability is low, i.e. where the absence of contact is the expected outcome rather than a paradox. Monte-Carlo exploration of the parameter space shows that, even when assuming a high frequency of habitable planets, the median Contact Probability across a wide range of parameter choices is under 0.42, and under 0.06 if we assume that habitable planets generally follow an "Earth-like" trajectory, with life requiring roughly 4.5 billion years to advance to Space Age. Thus, if Earth was a typical planet with regard to its evolutionary timeline, the Fermi Paradox would likely not be a paradox.
item.dc:creator: Philipp N. Spahn, Elmar Teufl

item.title: Six objects reported at 480 mph in a declassified military infrared video show brightness flicker at bird wingbeat rates
item.description: arXiv:2610.08692v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In September 2026 the U.S. Department of War released an infrared video recorded from a military aircraft over the Middle East, with a mission report describing six small spherical objects moving at an estimated 480 miles per hour. The brightness of each object, measured in every frame, rises and falls steadily at 7.1-7.9 times per second, each at its own rate and out of step with the others. Planted constant-brightness objects show that neither compression nor the sensor produces this flicker. The same analysis of the Galileo Project's ground-based infrared video finds flying animals beating at 3.4-10.0 times per second, within the range of bird wingbeats. An island in the opening frames provides a scale for the scene. A slow object at about three-quarters of the aircraft's height would appear to cross the sea surface at the reported speed, and would be at most about 0.3 meters across. The six objects are best explained as a small flock of birds. The same analysis finds similar beats, at 2.3-11.8 times per second, in 27 objects in twelve other released military videos. Releasing the redacted sensor and platform data would provide information that could refute the bird hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Haqq-Misra, Ravi Kopparapu, Richard Cloete, Omer Eldadi, Michael Shermer, Abraham Loeb
